hook: Solomon's path from electrical engineering to venture investment to AI partnerships at Airbus traces the evolution of applied AI from semiconductor and IoT adjacencies into aerospace's core technology strategy. At Airbus she shapes the partnerships and technology decisions that will determine how autonomous systems, AI-assisted design, and intelligent maintenance enter one of the most safety-critical industries in the world.
name: Reena Solomon

quote.text: Leading partnerships and technology strategy for AI and autonomy to shape the future of aerospace.

moniker: Head of AI Partnerships at Airbus, North America

reading.body:
Reena Solomon occupies a strategically significant position: she is the person at Airbus responsible for deciding which AI and autonomy partnerships enter one of the most regulated and safety-constrained manufacturing environments in existence.

Her career moves in a legible direction. She began in electrical engineering, moved through IoT and semiconductor investment scouting at SK Telecom Ventures, built a robotics initiative at Samsung from the ground up, and then spent time at an autonomous systems startup before arriving at Airbus. Each step added a layer, technical foundation first, then capital allocation, then corporate strategy at scale, then applied autonomy. The result is a profile built for exactly the role she now holds: translating external AI development into decisions a safety-critical organization can act on.

The data covers her background and current title but does not describe which specific partnerships she has formed at Airbus, which AI vendors or research institutions are involved, or how Airbus's internal technology adoption process works. The connection to compute infrastructure and power is not present in this data. What the record does show is how aerospace, an industry where certification timelines and failure consequences are extreme, is choosing to build its AI strategy: through a dedicated partnerships function staffed by someone whose entire background sits at the intersection of hardware, autonomy, and corporate venture.
